pos: n. (James Hog, c. 1658–1734, minister at Carnock, who republished The Marrow of Modern Divinity in Scotland)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob; Hog, a Scots surname, probably from the Old Norse byname.
biblical_def: James Hog was minister of Carnock in Fife, a man of long experience in the care of exercised souls and the author of practical treatises on the covenant of grace. In 1718 he reprinted in Edinburgh, with a commendatory preface, Edward Fisher's The Marrow of Modern Divinity, a seventeenth-century English dialogue that set the free offer of Christ against both legalism and antinomianism. The reprint lit the Marrow controversy. Principal James Hadow of St Andrews answered it, the General Assembly condemned several of its propositions in 1720, and twelve ministers, Hog at their head, lodged a representation defending it; they were rebuked in 1722 as the Marrow men. The quarrel was not academic. Hog and his brethren held that a sinner is invited to Christ as he is, and that any requirement of previous reformation turns the gospel into a law; their opponents feared the opposite error and suspected the book of loosening obedience. Hog had pastoral reasons for his stand: he had met too many who waited to be fit. “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). He died at Carnock in 1734, the year the Secession was formed, having never left the establishment himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marrow as the soft substance in the cavities of bones, and figuratively the essence or best part; and legalism is the reliance on works of law.
webster_full: MAR'ROW, n. A soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; the essence; the best part.
OF'FER, n. A proposal to be accepted or rejected; the act of presenting for acceptance.
PROP'OSITION, n. A proposal; that which is offered or affirmed.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Rom 10:4
For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
Gal 3:10
For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.
corruption_summary: The Carnock minister whose reprint of the Marrow began the controversy of 1718.
corruption_paragraphs: The error Hog fought has not gone away, only changed clothes. It now appears as the quiet assumption that a man must get his life in order before he may come to Christ, or that assurance is the reward of a tidy record rather than the fruit of resting on a finished work. Hog called this the legal frame, and he met it constantly in a parish of serious people.

The principle to recover is the order of the gospel itself: God justifies the ungodly, and faith is counted for righteousness to the man who works not (Rom 4:5). The invitation is addressed to the penniless — “he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat” (Isa 55:1) — and Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth (Rom 10:4).
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; asebes (G765), ungodly; telos (G5056), end, goal.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, justify; Romans 4:5.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, count, impute; Romans 4:5.
usage: “him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5) — the Marrow's whole case.
“he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat” (Isa 55:1) — the free offer.
“Christ is the end of the law for righteousness” (Rom 10:4) — against the legal frame.

pos: n. (the Auchterarder Creed, 1717, the disputed proposition put to licentiates by the presbytery of Auchterarder)
etymology: Gaelic uachdar ard, high upland; Latin credo, I believe.
biblical_def: The Auchterarder Creed was a single proposition which the presbytery of Auchterarder in Perthshire put to men seeking licence, to test whether they understood the order of the gospel. In its usual form it ran that it is not sound and orthodox to teach that we must forsake sin in order to our coming to Christ and instating us in covenant with God. William Craig refused it in 1717, complained to the General Assembly, and the Assembly condemned the proposition as unsound and detestable. Thomas Boston rose and said he believed it true, and from that moment the Marrow controversy had its occasion. The wording is clumsy and was meant to be narrow: the presbytery was not denying that repentance accompanies faith, nor that a converted man forsakes sin. It was denying that forsaking sin is a qualification a sinner must produce before Christ may be had — a condition which, once admitted, puts the law in the gospel's place and leaves the awakened conscience without a door. The question is settled in the invitation itself. “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). Christ does not ask the labouring man to lay down his load somewhere else first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief summary of the articles of Christian faith, and a condition as that which must exist before something else can take effect.
webster_full: CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a system of principles believed.
CONDI'TION, n. Terms of a contract; that which must exist as the occasion of something else.
FORSA'KE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
corruption_summary: The 1717 proposition that forsaking sin is no prerequisite to coming to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The error the creed was aimed at is the most natural error in religion and therefore the most durable. It survives wherever a seeker is told to clean himself up, settle his habits, or feel sufficiently sorry, and then come; and it survives in the gentler modern form which asks for a demonstrated commitment before Christ is offered at all. Either way the sinner is sent to the law for a ticket to the gospel.

The principle to recover is the plain terms of the call. “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (Joh 6:37) admits no preliminary. The forsaking of sin is the fruit of union with Christ and not the price of it; whoever reverses that order has, as the Marrow men said, made the gospel a new law.
roots_summary: Greek deute (G1205), come hither; ekballo (G1544), to cast out; Hebrew azab (H5800), to forsake.
roots_lines: Greek kopiao (G2872) — to labour to weariness; Matthew 11:28.
Greek phortizo (G5412) — to load, be heavy laden; Matthew 11:28.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, drive forth; John 6:37.
usage: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Mat 11:28) — the creed's warrant.
“him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (Joh 6:37) — no condition admitted.
“come ye, buy, and eat” (Isa 55:1) — what Craig would not sign.

pos: n. (John Simson, c. 1668–1740, professor of divinity at Glasgow, twice tried for error and finally suspended)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Simson, son of Simon.
biblical_def: John Simson held the chair of divinity at Glasgow from 1708 and taught a generation of Scottish ministers while his own orthodoxy was twice under judicial examination. The first process, begun by James Webster in 1714 and concluded in 1717, charged him with teaching that the heathen may be saved by the light of nature and with weakening the doctrine of original sin and of efficacious grace; the Assembly admonished him and forbade certain expressions. The second, from 1726, was graver: he was accused of denying the necessary existence and supreme deity of the Son, speaking of the Son's divinity in terms borrowed from the Arian controversy then running in England. In 1729 the General Assembly suspended him from teaching and preaching, a suspension never lifted, though his salary continued until his death in 1740. His two trials frame the Marrow controversy in time and explain its temperature: the same church that was arguing whether the gospel had been made too free was discovering that its divinity chair had made Christ less than God. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) was the clause his examiners kept returning to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion, and to suspend as to debar from any privilege for a time.
webster_full: HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine.
SUSPEND', v.t. To debar from any privilege, from the execution of an office, for a time.
PROFESS'OR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Joh 5:23
That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
Heb 1:8
But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.
Jude 1:4

For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: The Glasgow divinity professor suspended in 1729 for lowering the deity of the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: Simson's method is the one still used when a doctrine is to be abandoned without a denial: not a flat contradiction of the creed, but a habit of restating it in borrowed language, declining to use the church's own terms, and treating the hard clause as a matter on which a professor may suspend judgment. His students learned ambiguity, and some of them preached it.

The principle to recover is that honour withheld from the Son is honour withheld from the Father: “He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him” (Joh 5:23). Scripture addresses the Son as God outright — “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Heb 1:8) — and a teaching office which cannot say so plainly has already failed.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — word, reason, the Word; John 1:1.
usage: “the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — the clause at issue in 1726–29.
“He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father” (Joh 5:23) — the Assembly's ground.
“denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 1:4) — the charge at its height.

pos: n. (Gabriel Wilson, c. 1679–1750, minister at Maxton, one of the twelve Marrow men)
etymology: Hebrew Gabriel, man of God; Wilson, son of Will.
biblical_def: Gabriel Wilson was minister of Maxton in Roxburghshire and one of the twelve who signed the representation of 1721 in defence of the Marrow. He was among the most searching preachers of the group, and Thomas Boston reckoned him a man who understood the covenant of works better than most of its defenders. His particular labour was on the believer's relation to the law: he taught, with the Marrow, that a Christian is wholly free from the law as a covenant of works, having no righteousness to earn and no curse to fear there, and yet wholly bound to it as a rule of life in the hand of Christ. His opponents heard the first half and called it antinomianism; he answered that a man who is not free from the law as a covenant cannot keep it as a rule, because he is still working for wages. The distinction is Paul's own: “For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace” (Rom 6:14). Wilson stayed in the establishment when the four seceded in 1733, pleading with both sides, and died at Maxton in 1750.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberty as freedom from restraint, and bondage as slavery or involuntary subjection.
webster_full: LIB'ERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense.
BOND'AGE, n. Slavery or involuntary subjection to another.
RULE, n. That which is prescribed or laid down as a guide to conduct.
scriptures: Rom 6:14
For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
Gal 2:21
I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain.
corruption_summary: Maxton's minister on the law as covenant and the law as rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion Wilson addressed is as common now as then, and it runs both ways. One party hears that the believer is not under law and concludes that the commandments no longer bind; the other, fearing that conclusion, refuses to grant the freedom Paul plainly grants, and leaves Christians serving for a righteousness Christ has already provided. Both have collapsed two distinct uses of the law into one.

The principle to recover is Wilson's distinction. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1) is addressed to men who are also commanded to obey. To go back to the law for acceptance is to say that “if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain” (Gal 2:21).
roots_summary: Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; douleia (G1397), bondage; kurieuo (G2961), to have dominion.
roots_lines: Greek kurieuo (G2961) — to have dominion, lord it over; Romans 6:14.
Greek atheteo (G114) — to set aside, frustrate; Galatians 2:21.
usage: “ye are not under the law, but under grace” (Rom 6:14) — the law as covenant.
“be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1) — his warning to the legal frame.
“where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2Co 3:17) — and the law as rule follows.

pos: n. (James Fisher, 1697–1775, minister at Glasgow, co-author of Fisher's Catechism)
biblical_def: James Fisher was minister of Kinclaven, son-in-law of Ebenezer Erskine, and one of the four ministers deposed in 1733 who formed the Associate Presbytery; he afterwards served the Secession congregation in Glasgow for nearly forty years and taught its divinity students. His lasting work is the Assembly's Shorter Catechism Explained by Way of Question and Answer, begun with Ebenezer and Ralph Erskine and completed by Fisher, universally known as Fisher's Catechism. It takes each answer of the Shorter Catechism and opens it by further questions, so that a family or a class could work through the whole system of doctrine without a minister present; it carried the Marrow's free-offer theology into the plainest possible form and was used in Scottish, Irish and American homes for two centuries. Fisher's object was the one Paul names to Timothy, that the scriptures known from childhood are able to make a child wise unto salvation (2Ti 3:15). He also wrote in the Secession's defence against the establishment and against the Burgher oath, dying in Glasgow in 1775.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers, and to catechise as to instruct by asking questions.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers.
EXPLA'IN, v.t. To make plain, manifest or intelligible; to expound.
scriptures: And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: The Secession minister whose catechism taught Scotland its doctrine by question and answer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Catechising itself has largely been abandoned, on the assumption that memorised answers are a substitute for understanding and that children should be given stories rather than doctrine. Fisher's book answers that charge by its method: every memorised answer is immediately broken open by further questions, so the child who learns it is taught to reason from Scripture, not merely to recite.

The principle to recover is that doctrine is to be handed down deliberately, in the home as much as in the pulpit. “Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD” (Psa 34:11) is a programme of instruction, and a people so taught can “give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15).
roots_summary: Greek katecheo (G2727), to instruct by word of mouth; sophizo (G4679), to make wise; Hebrew lamad (H3925), to teach.
roots_lines: Greek katecheo (G2727) — to teach orally, catechise; Luke 1:4.
Greek brephos (G1025) — an infant, from a child; 2 Timothy 3:15.
Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train up, dedicate; Proverbs 22:6.
usage: “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — the catechism's aim.
“I will teach you the fear of the LORD” (Psa 34:11) — question and answer in the home.
“ready always to give an answer” (1Pe 3:15) — what the method produced.

pos: n. (William Wilson, c. 1690–1741, minister at Perth, one of the four founders of the Secession)
etymology: Old German Willahelm, resolute helmet; Perth, a Pictish place-name on the Tay.
biblical_def: William Wilson of Perth was one of the twelve Marrow men and one of the four ministers — with Ebenezer Erskine, Alexander Moncrieff and James Fisher — who were suspended in 1733 for protesting against the Assembly's handling of patronage and lay intrusion, and who in December of that year constituted the Associate Presbytery at Gairney Bridge. He was the presbytery's first professor of divinity and the ablest writer among the four; his defence of their secession argued that the Assembly, by settling ministers over unwilling congregations on the presentation of a patron, had taken from the Christian people a right Christ had given them, and that to acquiesce was to consent. He pressed the point from the apostles' answer before the council: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Wilson was no separatist by temper — the four always insisted they had seceded from the courts and not from the church — and he laboured to keep the new body confessional rather than merely aggrieved. He died at Perth in 1741, before the Burgher oath divided what he had helped to build.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines secession as the act of withdrawing, and patronage as the right of presentation to a church benefice.
webster_full: SECES'SION, n. The act of withdrawing, particularly from fellowship and communion.
PAT'RONAGE, n. The right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.
INTRU'SION, n. The act of thrusting in, or entering into a place without right.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: Perth's minister and the Associate Presbytery's first divinity professor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Wilson's case is routinely read backwards, as though the Secession were a quarrel about church politics. The issue was who gives a congregation its minister. Where a patron presents and a court installs over the heads of the people, the pastoral relation is created by property rather than by the call of Christ's flock, and the pulpit is answerable to the wrong master.

The principle to recover is that a steward is answerable to his Lord and must be found faithful there first (1Co 4:2), and that when courts and Christ's command diverge the apostolic answer stands: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Wilson accepted the reproach of going out “without the camp” (Heb 13:13) rather than consent.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; oikonomos (G3623), a steward; Hebrew nathib (H5410), a path.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Hebrew nathib (H5410) — a path, trodden way; Jeremiah 6:16.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the ground of the Secession.
“it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) — his view of the ministry.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — the four at Gairney Bridge.

pos: n. (Alexander Moncrieff, 1695–1761, minister at Abernethy, one of the four founders of the Secession)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Moncrieff, from the Perthshire place-name, the hill of the tree.
biblical_def: Alexander Moncrieff was laird of Culfargie and minister of Abernethy in Perthshire, a Marrow man and one of the four suspended in 1733. He had studied at Leyden under the elder Vitringa and brought to the Secession a strong grasp of the covenanting inheritance: for him the quarrel over patronage was of a piece with the Assembly's long retreat from the national covenants and from the church's liberty won in the previous century. He succeeded Wilson as professor of divinity to the Associate Presbytery, and in 1747, when the oath required of burgesses in several Scottish towns split the body, he went with the Antiburghers, holding that an oath to maintain the religion presently professed in the realm could not be sworn by men who judged that religion corrupt. His instinct throughout was conservative in the proper sense: not a preference for the past, but a refusal to let a boundary be moved quietly. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). He died at Abernethy in 1761.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land, and foundation as the basis or ground on which anything stands.
webster_full: LAND'MARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object.
FOUNDA'TION, n. The basis of an edifice; that on which any thing stands.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Abernethy's minister, Secession professor, and leader of the Antiburghers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Moncrieff is a useful corrective to the idea that the only danger to a church is an open denial. Nothing was ever formally repudiated in the Assembly he left; the covenants were simply not mentioned, the people's call was simply not enforced, and a generation grew up to whom these had never been doctrines at all. Boundaries are usually moved by silence.

The principle to recover is the question the psalm asks when the work is structural rather than doctrinal: “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3). The Antiburgher scruple about the burgess oath looks small until one remembers that an oath to uphold the religion as presently professed was, to Moncrieff, an oath against the very reformation he had seceded to preserve.
roots_summary: Hebrew gebul (H1366), a boundary; shathah (H8356), a foundation; nathib (H5410), a path.
roots_lines: Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, boundary, landmark; Proverbs 22:28.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — ancient, of long duration; Proverbs 22:28.
Hebrew harac (H2040) — to throw down, destroy; Psalm 11:3.
usage: “Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28) — his whole instinct.
“If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) — 1733.
“Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths” (Jer 6:16) — the Antiburgher case.

pos: n. (the Associate Presbytery, constituted 1733 at Gairney Bridge, the first court of the Scottish Secession)
etymology: Latin associare, to join to; Greek presbuterion, a body of elders.
biblical_def: The Associate Presbytery was constituted on 6 December 1733 at Gairney Bridge, near Kinross, by four ministers — Ebenezer Erskine, William Wilson, Alexander Moncrieff and James Fisher — who had been suspended by the Church of Scotland for protesting against the Assembly's settlement of ministers on patrons' presentations over congregations that did not want them. They did not claim to be a new church. They declared that they were seceding from the prevailing party in the courts, not from the Church of Scotland, whose confession, catechisms and government they held in full; and they offered to return the moment the grievances were redressed. The presbytery grew quickly, took in Ralph Erskine and others, erected its own divinity hall, and by 1745 had become the Associate Synod. In 1747 the oath required of burgesses in certain towns divided it into Burgher and Antiburgher synods, a breach not healed until 1820. Their constituting act rested on the simplest of grounds, that those who must walk together must first be agreed: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to associate as to join in company, and a presbytery as a body of elders in the Christian church.
webster_full: ASSO'CIATE, v.t. To join in company, as a friend, companion, partner or confederate.
PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of ministers and elders.
SECE'DE, v.i. To withdraw from fellowship, communion or association.
scriptures: Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: The court the four seceders constituted at Gairney Bridge in 1733.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Associate Presbytery is nevertheless badly served by both of the stories usually told about it. It was not a schism of the aggrieved, for the four held every article of the church they left and asked only that its own law be kept; and it was not a tidy new denomination, for it spent its first fifteen years insisting it was no such thing.

The principle to recover is that agreement precedes walking together, and that the agreement must be real (Amo 3:3). A communion maintained by not raising the question is not unity; and a church court which meets to consider a matter (Act 15:6) and then declines to consider it has already broken the fellowship it means to protect.
roots_summary: Hebrew ya'ad (H3259), to appoint, meet by agreement; Greek presbuterion (G4244), presbytery; episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together.
roots_lines: Hebrew ya'ad (H3259) — to appoint, meet by agreement; Amos 3:3.
Greek presbuterion (G4244) — the body of elders; 1 Timothy 4:14.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, book of remembrance; Malachi 3:16.
usage: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — Gairney Bridge.
“the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — what the Assembly would not do.
“they that feared the LORD spake often one to another” (Mal 3:16) — four ministers in a cottage.

pos: n. (Thomas Gillespie, 1708–1774, minister at Carnock, deposed in 1752 and founder of the Relief Church)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma, a twin; Gaelic gille easbuig, servant of the bishop.
biblical_def: Thomas Gillespie was ordained in England among the Independents at Doddridge's academy, then received into the Church of Scotland and settled at Carnock in 1741. In 1752 the General Assembly ordered the presbytery of Dunfermline to install an unwanted presentee at Inverkeithing; the presbytery refused, and the Assembly, needing an example, deposed Gillespie alone of the six — the only minister in the eighteenth century deposed by the Church of Scotland for such a refusal. He submitted without rancour, preached in a field and then in a barn to the people of Carnock who followed him, and for nine years stood alone. In 1761, joined by Thomas Boston the younger of Jedburgh and Thomas Colier of Colinsburgh, he constituted the Presbytery of Relief, so named because it was for the relief of Christians oppressed in their church privileges. His conduct through the whole affair was marked by a mildness that his judges did not expect, and he rested his case where Peter rested his: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to depose as to divest of office, and relief as the removal of any evil or burden.
webster_full: DEPO'SE, v.t. To divest of office; to deprive of an office or dignity.

corruption_summary: The only minister deposed by the Assembly for refusing to intrude a presentee.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Gillespie does expose a pattern in church courts which has not changed: when a court means to settle a disputed principle, it chooses the gentlest and least connected of the dissenters and makes an example of him, because the strong can retaliate and the mild cannot. Six men refused at Inverkeithing; one was deposed.

The principle to recover is that such a man is not thereby disqualified but blessed: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:10). Gillespie's nine years in a barn, and his refusal to answer in kind, were what made the Relief Church possible; his only boast was “the testimony of our conscience” (2Co 1:12).

pos: n. (the Presbytery of Relief, 1761–1847, the Scottish body formed for the relief of oppressed congregations)
etymology: Old French relever, to raise up again; Greek ekklesia, an assembly called out.
biblical_def: The Relief Church was constituted in 1761 as the Presbytery of Relief by Thomas Gillespie, Thomas Boston the younger and Thomas Colier, and took its name from its stated purpose: relief for Christians oppressed in their church privileges by the forced settlement of ministers. It held the Westminster standards but differed from the Secession in temper and in two practices. It declined to make the national covenants a term of communion, and it practised open communion, admitting to the Lord's table any believer of sound profession whatever his denomination — a position for which the Antiburghers called it lax and which made it, in fact, the most generous of the eighteenth-century Scottish bodies. Its congregations were numerous in the towns and it grew to over a hundred by 1800. In 1847 it united with the United Secession to form the United Presbyterian Church, which in 1900 joined the Free Church to make the United Free Church. Its founding temper was Paul's warning against judging another man's servant: “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth” (Rom 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines relief as the removal of any burden or oppression, and communion as fellowship, or the celebration of the Lord's supper.
webster_full: RELI'EF, n. The removal of any evil, grief, pain or oppression; alleviation.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the celebration of the Lord's supper.
OPPRESS'ION, n. The act of overburdening; hardship imposed on the weak.

corruption_summary: The open-communion Scottish body formed in 1761 for oppressed congregations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Relief is worth attention because it refused both of the available extremes. It would not stay in a church which installed ministers over unwilling flocks, and it would not make its own grievance into a boundary of the Lord's table. Its open communion was not indifference to doctrine, since it kept the Westminster standards for its own ministry; it was a judgment about who may eat.

The principle to recover is the one Paul applies to disputed matters among true brethren: “to his own master he standeth or falleth” (Rom 14:4). Liberty of that kind is not licence — “use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13) — and the Relief churches were among the most active in the towns they served.

usage: “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?” (Rom 14:4) — its open communion.

“by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13) — liberty without licence.
